Bandwidth, Transfer Time and TCP Throughput Calculator

Work out how long a transfer takes, how much bandwidth you need, and what TCP window size and round-trip time do to throughput.

2. How much bandwidth do I need?

3. Bandwidth-delay product and TCP throughput

Bits, bytes and why transfers feel slower than the link speed

Link speeds are quoted in bits per second (Mbps, Gbps) while file sizes are in bytes. There are 8 bits in a byte, so a 1 Gbps link moves at most 125 MB/s. Real transfers are slower because of Ethernet, IP and TCP headers, retransmissions, encryption, and the speed of the disks and CPUs at each end. The efficiency field accounts for this; 90% is a reasonable default for bulk TCP transfers on a clean link, and encrypted VPN tunnels often achieve less.

Decimal and binary units

Network speeds use decimal prefixes (1 Mbps = 1,000,000 bits/s). File sizes may be decimal (MB, GB) or binary (MiB, GiB, where 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes). The calculator supports both so you do not accumulate a 5–7% error converting between them.

Bandwidth-delay product and TCP window size

A TCP sender can only have one window of unacknowledged data in flight. The most it can send per round trip is the window size, so maximum throughput = window ÷ RTT. To fill a link you need a window at least equal to the bandwidth-delay product (bandwidth × RTT). On a 1 Gbps path with 80 ms of latency that is 10 MB. A default 64 KiB window would cap throughput at about 6.5 Mbps, which is why long fat networks need TCP window scaling and well-tuned buffers.

Packet loss and the Mathis estimate

Even a small amount of loss limits classic TCP, because each loss makes the sender slow down. The Mathis formula estimates throughput as roughly MSS ÷ (RTT × √loss) × 1.22. The tool shows this as a ceiling so you can see how much a lossy WAN link or wireless hop costs at a given RTT.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to transfer 1 TB over a 1 Gbps link?

At 100% efficiency about 2 hours 13 minutes; at 90% about 2 hours 28 minutes. Use section 1 above with your own numbers.

What efficiency should I use?

90–94% for local wired TCP transfers, 70–85% over a VPN or high-latency WAN, and lower for Wi-Fi. If you have measurements from iperf, use those.

Why is my throughput limited on a high-latency link?

Most often the TCP window is smaller than the bandwidth-delay product, or there is packet loss. Compare the maximum throughput for your window with the link speed in section 3.

What is the difference between Mbps and MB/s?

Mbps is megabits per second; MB/s is megabytes per second. Divide Mbps by 8 to get MB/s.
